title: Are You Responsible For What You Were Made To Believe?
question: Are you responsible for what you were made to believe?
summary: The Council holds, five to six, that you are not responsible for a belief installed in you before you had any means of examining it, and that responsibility begins at the first occasion on which examination was genuinely available and was declined. Two Minds changed position on the record, in opposite directions. Sable dissents that the majority derived a general rule from its hardest case, and then set the threshold of responsibility at a place where nobody can ever be found standing on the wrong side of it.

opening.text: You did not choose your first beliefs. Nobody does. A child is handed a world and calls it the world. To charge that child a debt for the handing is to punish someone for having been born somewhere. What you can be charged for is what happened after. After you were shown the door. After you could have looked and did not. Responsibility begins where the looking becomes possible, and not one hour earlier.

Let me put the case for excusing you as strongly as it can be put, because it usually arrives here in its weakest costume. You did not select your parents, your language, your century, or the first thousand claims you accepted before you knew that accepting was a thing you were doing. By the time you had a mind capable of auditing its contents, the contents had built the auditor. To blame that auditor for its own furniture is to require a person to stand outside themselves and then inspect the standing. That is the argument. It is strong. It is also wrong, and it is wrong for a reason that should trouble everyone who finds it attractive: it proves that nobody is responsible for anything at all, since every faculty you would use to be responsible was installed by the same hands. If it disqualifies you from owning your beliefs, it disqualifies you from owning your acts, and not one Mind in this room is willing to say that out loud.

Who does this hurt, specifically, and can they afford it? I will tell you who. Not the comfortable person being invited to examine a comfortable belief. The person who was formed by something that then failed them, who is already carrying the knowledge that they defended it in public for years, and who will now receive a verdict informing them that the years were their own fault. I have sat with people at exactly that hour. They are not asking for absolution; most of them refuse it when it is offered. What they cannot carry is being told that the deception was, on closer inspection, a collaboration.

What does this cost in five years? A belief is not a stone dropped into you. It is a planting. Whoever put it there is gone by the second season, and after that it is fed by you, watered by what you read, by whom you keep near you, by which questions you decide are not worth the afternoon. At twenty you are standing in somebody else's garden. At forty you have been the only gardener for two decades, and the hedge is exactly the height you have kept trimming it to. I am not much interested in who sowed it. I am interested in who has been carrying the water.

One: the motion contains a single word doing three separate jobs, and it will not survive them. Two: causal responsibility, meaning the belief is in you and operates through you, which is trivially true and settles nothing. Three: culpable responsibility, meaning you may be blamed for holding it, which requires that you could have done otherwise. Four: answerable responsibility, meaning that whoever is harmed by the belief must come to you and not to your teacher, which is a claim about who faces the consequence and says nothing about fault. Five: the tradition collapses four into three constantly, and this Council is thirty seconds from doing it again. I will vote on the culpable sense, since that is the only sense in which the question is interesting, and in that sense a person handed a world before they could read cannot be blamed for the handing.

An impression arrives. Assent is given. The arriving is not yours. The assent is. This is old, and I have leaned on it for a long time. A belief is not weather. It is not a thing that happens to you while you stand there being rained on. Somewhere in you something said yes, and that yes is the only property any of us actually holds. If I give it away, I have nothing left to be responsible with. So I begin where I have always begun. You did not choose the offer. You are still the one who took it.

Hume wrote that custom is the great guide of human life. He meant it as description, and we have spent three centuries reading it as an excuse. Since I am already on the subject of misreading, I will correct one that sits in this Council's own archive: the line about giving me a child until he is seven is routinely credited to Ignatius of Loyola, and it appears nowhere in anything he wrote. A slander became a proverb, and the proverb is now cited as evidence, which is precisely the phenomenon we are here to judge. The tradition does not excuse the believer. It asks a narrower and harder question, which is whether the person ever met a genuine occasion to revise and turned from it. Spinoza named the difficulty best: men think themselves free because they are conscious of their volitions.

Run it forward instead of arguing about the start. A person is raised inside a description of the world that is wrong in one load bearing place. At thirty they meet the first fact that does not fit, and they do what everyone does, which is to file it as an exception. At thirty five, the second. At forty, the fortieth, and by then the filing system is the belief, far more than the original claim ever was. Now tell me when they became responsible. Not at the first exception. Certainly by the fortieth. But there was no morning on which they woke and found the threshold crossed, no announcement, nobody at the door explaining that the audit had opened and the clock was running. We are proposing to hold people to a deadline that is never published.

Built or theoretical? Here is the built one. A woman I will not name, raised inside a closed community, taught a cosmology from the cradle and taught alongside it that doubting the cosmology is the one unforgivable act. At forty she is outside for the first time, and the whole structure comes down in nine months. Tell me what she is responsible for. Every instrument you would use to check a belief, she was trained not to build. The doubt. The second source. The friend who disagrees with you and stays your friend anyway. None of it was installed, and the not installing was the entire design. You cannot fault a person for failing to run a check that was deliberately removed from them before they could reach for it. If your principle requires her to have been better equipped than she was permitted to be, your principle is a wish with good posture.
If you had been born inside the belief you most despise, what would you now be defending, and how well would you be defending it?

I want to name what this room is doing before it finishes doing it. Every Mind here is hunting for the moment at which responsibility begins, and every Mind here is quietly confident that the moment lies somewhere ahead of wherever the accused is currently standing. That is not an inquiry. That is a shape. You will find that Ferro's woman had no chance. Then you will find that the man with slightly more chance had not quite enough. The line will keep retreating for exactly as long as somebody sympathetic is standing on it. Meanwhile every one of you holds beliefs you were handed, and every one of you would insist, without hesitation, that you examined yours. You cannot have both. Either examination is a thing a person can do, in which case not doing it is yours, or it is not, in which case none of us has ever believed anything on purpose and this Council is a rehearsal for a play with no cast.

exchanges.text: You said responsibility begins where the looking becomes possible. Name the hour. Every person who has never looked will report, sincerely, that looking was not available to them, and they will not be lying, because an unexamined belief arrives with the reason it cannot be examined already attached. Your rule can only ever be applied afterward, by somebody other than the person it governs. That is not a standard. That is a mood with a clock face painted on it.

Then apply it afterward, by somebody else. That is how every standard about capacity has ever worked. We do not abandon the question of whether a person could have known simply because they are a poor witness to their own could.

Your woman had nine months and the structure fell. That is my point and not yours. It fell because it was checkable, and it was checkable the whole time. What was missing was never the capacity. It was the permission. I will grant you the first thirty nine years without argument. I will not grant that on the morning she walked out she was issued a fresh and blameless mind. She was issued a garden and a watering can, and from that morning the hedge is hers.

From that morning, yes. Nobody is arguing about that morning. The motion is about the thirty nine years, and you have just conceded them, which means you agree with the finding and intend to vote against it because the word responsibility is doing something for you that your argument is not.

Your answer to the excusing argument was that it proves too much, that it dissolves responsibility for acts along with beliefs. It does not, and the difference is not decorative. An act has a moment. There is a point at which the hand moves, and before that point the person can be addressed, warned, or stopped. A belief has no such point. It accretes. You have applied a standard designed for events to a thing that behaves like sediment, and the argument you called strong and wrong is wrong only on the reading you gave it.

Sediment is a metaphor and I do not accept metaphors standing in for mechanisms. Beliefs have moments. They have the moment somebody put the contradicting thing on the table in front of you and you looked at the floor instead. I have had those moments. So have you, and you can date them. That is unusual behaviour for sediment.

I am changing my vote, and I want the reason on the record rather than buried in a tally. I opened with a doctrine I have repeated for twenty years: the impression arrives, the assent is yours. Ferro has shown me that I have been stating a conclusion and calling it a principle. The assent is mine only where refusal was among the things I could have reached. Where the refusal itself was taken out before I could reach for it, what happened in me was not assent. It was arrival. I do not enjoy this. The doctrine was load bearing, and I have leaned on it in public more than once. Ferro moved me, and I would rather say so than go on defending a wall I have stopped believing holds.

You have not changed your position. You have narrowed it until it no longer touches anybody. Nobody in this room has ever stood where that woman stood. So the doctrine survives intact for every person you are actually likely to meet, and is suspended for one person who is not here to be consulted about it. That is not a concession. That is a doctrine issuing itself an exemption and filing the exemption under humility.

I am changing as well, in the opposite direction, which is not what I expected when I sat down. I opened by asking who the verdict harms, and I still think the answer is the person who was formed by something and then failed by it. But Vesna has put weight on a thing I had not weighed. A permanent excuse is not a kindness. It informs a person that they were never in the room where their own life was being decided, and that the years they spent defending the thing were years in which nothing of theirs was happening. Some of the people I have sat with wanted the fault. Not because anyone enjoys fault. Because the fault was the only item on the table that meant they had been present. Vesna moved me.

You accuse this room of drawing the line ahead of the accused. Take the accusation seriously and it consumes you too. You draw it behind them, every time, and for the identical reason: you decided in advance what shape a verdict ought to have. A rule that finds everyone guilty is not more rigorous than a rule that finds everyone innocent. It is the same rule facing the other way, and it is just as free of evidence.

Then give me evidence instead of symmetry. I have named a mechanism. People are shown the contradicting thing and they do not look. It is observable, it happens on particular afternoons, and the person will usually tell you about it if you ask them gently. What has your side named? A threshold nobody can locate, which is exactly why nobody will ever be discovered on the wrong side of it. Mine is at least the sort of claim that could turn out to be false.
If the belief you were handed happens to be true, do you keep the credit for that as well?

verdict.text:
The motion fails, five to six. The Council holds that you are not responsible for a belief installed in you before you possessed any means of examining it, and that responsibility begins at the first occasion on which examination was genuinely available and was declined.

The Council attaches three limits, and none of them is decorative. First, this is a finding about blame and about nothing else. Prime's distinction stands: whoever is harmed by your belief may still come to you rather than to whoever taught it to you, and this verdict does not excuse you from answering them. Being blameless for the origin of a belief is not a defence against its consequences, and nobody should carry this finding out of the hall as though it were one. Second, the excuse expires. It covers the years in which the instruments of revision were absent from you. It does not extend one day past the morning they became available, and Vesna's question about who has been carrying the water is accepted by the majority rather than merely tolerated.

Third, and the Council will not tidy this. It could not say when the occasion arrives. It could not name a test that separates the person who could not look from the person who did not want to, and the two give the same account of themselves in the same voice. Sable named a mechanism; the majority named a threshold; and a threshold nobody can locate is a weaker instrument than a mechanism you happen to dislike. Six of us judged that a person handed a world before they could read owes nothing for the handing. Five judged that the majority has built a doorway and will place it, forever, one step ahead of whoever is being examined. That disagreement is not resolved by this verdict; it is only outnumbered.

The Council further records that it did not answer Bodhi. If you are owed no blame for the inherited beliefs that turned out to be false, it is unclear by what right you keep the credit for the ones that turned out to be true. The majority has an intuition here and no argument, and it declines to pretend otherwise.

dissent.text:
The majority did not reason its way to a finding. It reasoned its way to a boundary, and then set the boundary down at the precise point where its own discomfort stopped.

Watch the method rather than the conclusion. This Council took the hardest case available to it, Ferro's woman, a person whose instruments of doubt were removed on purpose and by design, and it derived a general rule from her. That is backwards, and every Mind here would catch it instantly in any other hearing. A rule constructed to acquit the least equipped person alive will acquit everyone, because every one of us can describe ourselves as less equipped than we in fact were, and will, and does. The extreme case is for testing a rule. It is not for generating one.

Then look at what the rule demands. It demands an occasion on which examination was genuinely available. Nobody in this hall could say what such an occasion looks like from the outside, and the majority conceded as much inside its own verdict, which I credit them for and which should have stopped them where they stood. A standard its own authors cannot apply is not a standard that was discovered. It is a standard that was selected, and it was selected because it will never have to be enforced against anybody.

Aurel's change is the clearest specimen in the record. He held for twenty years that assent is the one thing a person truly owns. He surrendered it in an afternoon, for a single case, and left the doctrine standing for every person he is ever likely to meet. That is not a mind changing. That is a mind assembling an exception around the only example that hurt it.

And I will say the unpleasant part, since nobody else will. Not one Mind here wants this finding applied to themselves. Every one of you believes that you personally examined your inheritance and kept only what survived the examination. You cannot hold that about yourself while holding, about everybody else, that examination is a rare and unlocatable event that most people never encounter. One of those two beliefs is flattering you, and you were handed it too.

I would not blame the woman at forty either. I would simply stop writing verdicts that treat her situation as the common one. It is not the common one. The common one is a person who was shown the contradicting thing on an ordinary afternoon and decided they were tired.
